title: Excellence in all things
hook: a blade being sharpened, and the odd place a hadith chose to talk about excellence

segments.voice: Yesterday, qana'ah, and your line: rich in the soul. And a week closes today: pardon and overlook, gentleness, justice, the ties of kin, loving for others, contentment. Now the virtue that runs underneath all of them. Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.
screen: `RICH IN THE SOUL.` · `A WEEK OF VIRTUES.`

segments.voice: Where would you expect a teaching on excellence? A prayer hall, maybe, or a workshop. Not a blade being sharpened for an animal that's about to become a family's meal. Of all the moments to talk about excellence, this seems an odd one. But that's where the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, chose to put it. In Sahih Muslim, Shaddad ibn Aws reports him saying, in paraphrase: Allah has prescribed ihsan, excellence, in all things. So when you kill, kill well, and when you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each of you sharpen his blade and spare the animal suffering. Today: excellence, starting with the blade.
screen: `A BLADE BEING SHARPENED.` → `AN ODD PLACE FOR EXCELLENCE.` → `PRESCRIBED IN ALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: The word is ihsan: doing a thing beautifully, doing it well. In the hadith of Jibril, in Sahih Muslim, ihsan is described as worshipping Allah as though you see Him, and though you don't see Him, He sees you. That's ihsan in prayer. Today's hadith carries it out of the prayer hall. First, the verb. The hadith says Allah kataba ihsan: wrote it, prescribed it. It's the same verb as in the fasting verse of al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's words: "Fasting is prescribed for you." So in this hadith, excellence isn't extra credit. It's written in. Second, the example. Of everything the hadith could have picked, it picks a moment where cutting corners costs someone who can't complain. The animal can't object. Excellence here means care for the one with no voice: a sharp blade, no drawn-out pain. Third, the reach: in all things. If slaughter can be done with ihsan, so can a spreadsheet, a diaper change, an email, a pile of laundry. Ask who is on the other end of the task, and make it easier on them. Fourth, the week. Pardon done with ihsan doesn't keep a ledger. Justice done with ihsan is gentle. Ties kept with ihsan don't wait to be repaid. Loving for others with ihsan means the good, not just the polite. So ihsan isn't one more virtue on the list. It's the way every virtue on the list gets done. Not perfection. Doing the thing well, because He sees.
screen: `AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.` · `KATABA: WRITTEN IN, NOT EXTRA.` · `CARE FOR THE ONE WITH NO VOICE.` · `HOW EVERY VIRTUE GETS DONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: do one thing excellently. Settle, and breathe. Choose one ordinary task waiting for you after the bell. Washing a pan. Writing a reply. Making the bed. Picture doing it well, not just fast. The blade sharpened, so to speak: the right tool, your full attention, the last corner done. Then ask who will meet the result of this task, and how it could be easier on them. If you pray, you can hold the hadith of Jibril in mind: as though you see Him, and He sees you. The bell holds the time.
Excellence in all things. Ihsan: doing each thing beautifully and well, prescribed, the hadith says, right down to a sharpened blade. Today's word.

Your line: excellence in everything. Today, do one ordinary task as if it mattered completely, and finish the last corner. Tomorrow, inward path close: the whole road so far. Day one thousand three hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Muslims learn ihsan from the hadith of Jibril, worshipping Allah as though you see Him, and apply the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws to everyday work, including slaughter with a sharp blade and without needless suffering.

pairs: doing a thing beautifully and well

myth: the hadith of excellence uses slaughter as its example
when you slaughter, slaughter well: sharpen the blade, spare the animal.
the hadith limits ihsan to prayer and worship
Allah has prescribed ihsan in all things.
the hadith's verb for prescribed is the fasting verse's verb
kataba: 'Fasting is prescribed for you,' al-Baqarah 2:183.

fork.setup: you're about to slaughter an animal for a family meal. the hadith of Shaddad ibn Aws speaks to exactly this. what does it ask?
options: sharpen your blade and spare the animal suffering.
fork.reveal: Sahih Muslim: Allah has prescribed ihsan in all things. so slaughter well: sharpen the blade, and spare the animal.

original.note: Arabic: excellence, doing a thing beautifully and well.

trapdoor: what you thought: excellence means being the best.
what it means: ihsan is doing each thing beautifully and well, as though you see Allah, knowing He sees you.
what a scholar hears: Muslim 1955 ('kataba al-ihsana 'ala kulli shay'') beside the hadith of Jibril: ihsan is a level of faith and a way of doing every task.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1955 (Shaddad ibn Aws: Allah has prescribed ihsan in all things; slaughter well, sharpen the blade)
Sahih Muslim 8 (the hadith of Jibril: ihsan is to worship Allah as though you see Him)

notes: Hadith numbers to confirm: Muslim 1955 (Shaddad ibn Aws); Muslim 8 (hadith of Jibril).
Pickthall 2:183: confirm 'Fasting is prescribed for you'.
Teach links the hadith's kataba to kutiba in 2:183; confirm the grammatical framing is acceptable.
Week-end review names the week's virtues (days 1310–1315); 'pardon and overlook' is day 1310's line.
